2 The arc-topology (2.1 Properties of arc-covers, 2.2 Relation to submersions)
3 Studying v-sheaves via valuation rings (3.1 Finitary v-sheaves, 3.2 Ultraproducts and sheaves, 3.3 Detection of universal F-descent, 3.4 Detection in the v-topology)
4 The main result for arc-descent (4.1 Aic-v-excision and arc-descent, 4.2 Aic-v-excision and excision, 4.3 Excision via arc-sheafification)
5 Examples of arc-sheaves (5.1 Étale cohomology, 5.2 Constructible étale sheaves, 5.3 Differential forms in characteristic zero, 5.4 Perfect schemes of characteristic p > 0)
6 Consequences of arc-descent (6.1 Formal glueing squares, 6.2 GAGA for rigid étale cohomology of affinoids, 6.3 A variant of excision)
7 An application: Artin–Grothendieck vanishing in rigid geometry

summary: Bhatt and Mathew introduce the arc-topology on schemes: a map of qcqs schemes is an arc-cover when every map from a rank ≤ 1 valuation ring lifts after an extension of rank ≤ 1 valuation rings. It refines the v-topology (the pro-version of Voevodsky's h-topology), agrees with it over noetherian bases, and is exactly the class of universally spectrally submersive maps. Their main theorem characterises arc-descent: a finitary v-sheaf valued in an ∞-category compactly generated by cotruncated objects is an arc-sheaf if and only if it is excisive for Milnor squares, if and only if it satisfies one excision square for each absolutely integrally closed valuation ring and each prime of it. The proof detects descent by ultraproducts and by absolutely integrally closed valuation rings and then runs an induction over the intervals of the totally ordered spectrum of a valuation ring. Étale cohomology with torsion coefficients, bounded constructible complexes, Rydh's categories of étale objects, Huber–Jörder h-differentials and perfect complexes on perfect F_p-schemes are all arc-sheaves; on perfect schemes the arc-covers are exactly the universally effective epimorphisms. Consequently every arc-sheaf satisfies excision and formal glueing, which yields new proofs of the Gabber–Huber affine analogue of proper base change (in a large class of examples) and of the Fujiwara–Gabber theorem, a GAGA theorem for the étale cohomology of proper rigid spaces, and Artin–Grothendieck vanishing for affinoids over a complete algebraically closed nonarchimedean field, extending results of Hansen. The atlas has nothing in this direction. SchemeAndStackFoundations owns the Zariski, étale, fppf and pro-étale sites of schemes and fpqc descent; the v-topology it plans (DiamondsAndVStacks D2) is Scholze's v-topology on perfectoid spaces and diamonds, a different site. No layer defines the h-, v- or arc-topology on schemes, the ∞-categorical descent formalism used here, excision or formal glueing for étale cohomology, or the rigid-analytic vanishing theorem; the paper's general-purpose pieces — spectral submersions, sheaves on profinite sets, ultraproducts of rings and Milnor squares — do have owners, and are routed to them.

items.name: Valuation rings and extensions of valuation rings
items.statement: A valuation ring is an integral domain in which for any two elements one divides the other; an extension of valuation rings is a faithfully flat map V → W of valuation rings, equivalently an injective local homomorphism. The rank of a valuation ring is the Krull dimension of its spectrum, which is a totally ordered set.
items.note: Mathlib has valuation rings as domains with total divisibility, with the value group and the total order on ideals; 'extension of valuation rings' in the paper's sense (faithfully flat, equivalently injective and local) is not a Mathlib definition but is immediate from it.

items.name: Grothendieck topologies, sites and sheaves
items.statement: A Grothendieck topology on a category assigns to each object a collection of covering sieves closed under base change, local character and containing the maximal sieve; a pretopology generates one from covering families; a presheaf is a sheaf when the sheaf axiom holds for every covering.
items.note: The 1-categorical theory of sites, sheaves and sheafification is in Mathlib; what the paper needs beyond it is the ∞-categorical sheaf axiom (a totalization), which is not.

items.name: Spectral spaces, spectral maps and the constructible topology
items.statement: A topological space is spectral if it is T0, quasi-compact, sober, quasi-separated and its quasi-compact opens form a basis closed under finite intersection; a spectral map is a continuous map whose preimages of quasi-compact opens are quasi-compact; the constructible topology is generated by the quasi-compact opens and their complements, and a surjective spectral map induces a quotient map for the constructible topology.
items.note: Mathlib has spectral spaces, spectral maps and the constructible topology as a type synonym; the statement that a surjective spectral map is a constructible quotient map, used in Remark 2.15, is not in the library.

items.name: Ultrafilters and the Stone–Čech compactification
items.statement: An ultrafilter on a set T is a collection of subsets not containing ∅, closed under finite intersections, and containing T' or T \ T' for every T' ⊂ T; each t ∈ T gives the principal ultrafilter of subsets containing t. The set βT of all ultrafilters on T is a profinite space, the Stone–Čech compactification of T with the discrete topology, T ↪ βT is an open embedding with dense image, and the Boolean algebra of clopens of βT is the power set of T.
items.note: Mathlib has ultrafilters and the Stone–Čech compactification of a topological space; the identification of the clopen algebra of βT with the power set of T, which the paper uses to turn presheaves on P(T) into sheaves on βT, is not in the library.

items.name: Étale cohomology of schemes and its base-change theorems
items.statement: For a torsion étale sheaf on a scheme, RΓ(X_ét, F) is defined, satisfies étale descent, proper base change and proper cohomological descent (so that proper surjections are of universal descent for RΓ(−_ét, A) with A torsion).
items.locator: arXiv:1807.04725v4 (14 December 2020), Example 1.6, Example 3.3 and Proposition 5.2
items.note: SF.2 owns the Zariski, étale, fppf and pro-étale sites of schemes with sheaf cohomology, localization and proper/smooth base change; EDC.0 owns the constructible coefficient interfaces. The paper uses these as known inputs.

items.name: fpqc descent and algebraic spaces
items.statement: Effective descent along faithfully flat quasi-compact covers, and the theory of algebraic spaces with representable diagonals, in particular the equivalence between constructible étale sheaves of sets on X and étale quasi-compact quasi-separated algebraic spaces over X.
items.locator: arXiv:1807.04725v4 (14 December 2020), Theorem 5.6(3) (citing [Mil80, Ch. V, Thm. 1.5] and [SGA4, Exp. IX, Cor. 2.7.1])
items.note: SF.1 plans effective fpqc/fppf descent and algebraic spaces; the identification of constructible sheaves of sets with étale algebraic spaces is the input Rydh's theorem is stated with.

items.name: Artin–Grothendieck vanishing
items.statement: Let k be a separably closed field and ℓ a prime invertible in k, A a finitely generated k-algebra of dimension d, and F an ℓ-power torsion étale sheaf on Spec(A). Then H^j(Spec(A), F) = 0 for j > d.
items.locator: arXiv:1807.04725v4 (14 December 2020), Theorem 7.1 ([SGA4, Exp. XIV, Cor. 3.2])
items.note: EDC.4 consumes 'the imported affine Artin vanishing theorem' and EDC.5 proves its perverse form; the atlas's roadmap text attributes ownership of Artin vanishing to the pinned EtaleBaseChange packet of the CohomologicalPointCounting family, which has no stage in the atlas extracts. Recorded as planned against the layers that name it; a reviewer may prefer to treat the classical statement as unowned.

items.name: v-covers and the v-topology
items.statement: A map of quasi-compact quasi-separated (qcqs) schemes Y → X is a v-cover if for every valuation ring V and every map Spec(V) → X there is an extension of valuation rings V → W and a map Spec(W) → Y making the square with Spec(W) → Spec(V) → X commute. The v-topology on schemes has as covering families {f_i : Y_i → X} those such that for every affine open V ⊂ X there are a finite set K, a map t : K → I and affine opens U_k ⊂ f_{t(k)}^{-1}(V) with ⊔_k U_k → V a v-cover.
items.note: The v-topology on qcqs schemes (the pro-version of Voevodsky's h-topology). The atlas has the v-topology only on perfectoid spaces and diamonds (DiamondsAndVStacks D2), which is a different site with a different covering condition.

items.name: arc-covers and the arc-topology
items.statement: A map f : Y → X of qcqs schemes is an arc-cover if for every rank ≤ 1 valuation ring V and every map Spec(V) → X there is an extension V → W of rank ≤ 1 valuation rings and a map Spec(W) → Y lifting Spec(W) → Spec(V) → X. The arc-topology on schemes is defined from arc-covers exactly as the v-topology is defined from v-covers.
items.note: The central definition of the paper: covers are tested only against rank ≤ 1 valuation rings, i.e. arcs. Nothing in the atlas defines it.

items.name: A rank-two valuation ring gives an arc-cover that is not a v-cover
items.statement: Let V be a valuation ring of rank 2 with unique height 1 prime p. Then V_p and V/p are rank 1 valuation rings and V → V_p × V/p is an arc-cover but not a v-cover; if f ∈ V − p is a nonunit then V → V_f × V/fV is a finitely presented arc-cover that is not a v-cover.
items.note: The example separating the two topologies, and the model for the excision squares of Proposition 2.8.

items.name: Reduction to qcqs schemes
items.statement: A contravariant functor on all schemes which is a Zariski sheaf is determined by its restriction to qcqs schemes, and every Zariski sheaf on qcqs schemes comes from a unique Zariski sheaf on schemes; since the arc-topology is finer than the Zariski topology and is finitary on qcqs schemes, one may work throughout with qcqs schemes.
items.note: The convention that makes the sheaf conditions checkable; 'finitary' is in the sense of [SAG, §A.3.1].

items.name: ∞-categorical descent and τ-sheaves
items.statement: For a presheaf F : Sch_qcqs^op → C valued in an ∞-category, F satisfies descent for Y → X if F(X) → lim(F(Y) ⇉ F(Y ×_X Y) ⇛ …) is an equivalence (a totalization over the simplex category). If this holds for every cover of a topology τ and F carries finite disjoint unions to finite products, F satisfies τ-descent, i.e. is a τ-sheaf.
items.note: The ∞-categorical sheaf axiom; Mathlib's sheaf theory is 1-categorical and has no totalizations of cosimplicial objects.

items.name: τ-cohomology is a τ-sheaf
items.statement: For a Grothendieck topology τ on schemes (of suitably bounded cardinality if τ is large), a scheme X and a coefficient ring Λ, the functor F(X) = RΓ(X_τ, Λ) valued in the derived ∞-category D(Λ) is a τ-sheaf.
items.note: The formal statement that cohomology on a site satisfies descent for that site; it is the reason the paper's theorems about arc-sheaves apply to étale cohomology.

items.name: Criteria for arc-descent
items.statement: Let F : Sch_qcqs^op → D(Z)^{≥0} be finitary, i.e. F takes filtered limits with affine transition maps to filtered colimits. Then F is an arc-sheaf if and only if F is a v-sheaf and for every valuation ring V with algebraically closed fraction field and every prime p ⊂ V the square F(Spec V) → F(Spec V/p), F(Spec V_p) → F(Spec κ(p)) is cartesian.
items.note: The main criterion: arc-descent is v-descent plus one excision square for absolutely integrally closed valuation rings.

items.name: arc-descent for étale cohomology and for constructible complexes
items.statement: For a finite ring Λ, the assignment X ↦ D^b_cons(X, Λ), the bounded derived ∞-category of sheaves of Λ-modules on X_ét with constructible cohomology, satisfies arc-descent; in particular X ↦ RΓ(X_ét, Λ) is an arc-sheaf.
items.note: The headline example; everything in Section 6 is a consequence of it.

items.name: arc-descent for perfect complexes on perfect schemes
items.statement: On qcqs F_p-schemes, the functor X ↦ Perf(X_perf) satisfies arc-descent.
items.note: The second main example, extending v-descent for perfect complexes on perfect schemes.

items.name: Characterisation of arc-covers of perfect schemes
items.statement: On qcqs perfect F_p-schemes, a map Y → X is an arc-cover if and only if it is a universally effective epimorphism in the category of qcqs perfect F_p-schemes.
items.note: Identifies the arc-topology with the canonical topology in the perfect setting.

items.name: Excision data, Milnor squares and excisive functors
items.statement: An excision datum is a map f : (A, I) → (B, J) of pairs of commutative rings with ideals such that f carries I isomorphically onto J; the resulting square A → A/I, B → B/J is both cartesian and cocartesian (a Milnor square). A D(Z)-valued functor F on commutative rings is excisive if it carries every such square to a cartesian square, equivalently if fib(F(A) → F(A/I)) → fib(F(B) → F(B/J)) is an equivalence.
items.note: Milnor squares and excision are the subject of GeneralAlgebraicKTheory K.5, which plans relative K-theory of a pair and excision under hypotheses; this paper is a source for that layer and the arc-topology roadmap should import the notion.

items.name: arc-sheaves are excisive
items.statement: Let C be an ∞-category with all small limits. Any arc-sheaf F : Sch_qcqs^op → C satisfies excision.
items.locator: arXiv:1807.04725v4 (14 December 2020), Theorem 1.12 (= Theorem 4.1 and Corollary 4.25)
items.note: One of the two consequences advertised in the abstract: glueing conditions such as excision in the sense of algebraic K-theory are forced by arc-descent.

items.name: v-descent alone does not give excision
items.statement: The hypothesis that F be an arc-sheaf and not merely a v-sheaf is essential: general v-sheaves can fail to be excisive. For an excision datum (A, I) → (B, J) the map Spec(B) ⊔ Spec(A/I) → Spec(A) is always an arc-cover but not in general a v-cover; with V a rank 2 valuation ring and p its height 1 prime, (V, p) → (V_p, pV_p) is such an example.
items.note: The observation that led the authors to the arc-topology.

items.name: Formal glueing data
items.statement: A formal glueing datum is a pair (R → S, I) with I ⊂ R a finitely generated ideal such that R/I^n ≅ S/I^nS for all n ≥ 0. A contravariant functor F on schemes satisfies formal glueing if it carries the square Spec(S) \ V(IS) → Spec(S), Spec(R) \ V(I) → Spec(R) to a cartesian square.
items.note: The Beauville–Laszlo style glueing square; the atlas has no layer for it.

items.name: arc-sheaves satisfy formal glueing
items.statement: Let C be an ∞-category with all small limits. Any arc-sheaf F : Sch_qcqs^op → C satisfies formal glueing.
items.locator: arXiv:1807.04725v4 (14 December 2020), Theorem 1.15 (= Theorem 6.4 and Corollary 6.7)
items.note: The second consequence advertised in the abstract.

items.name: v-descent alone does not give formal glueing
items.statement: As for excision, the arc-hypothesis is essential: for a formal glueing datum (R → S, I) the map Spec(S) ⊔ (Spec(R) \ V(I)) → Spec(R) is an arc-cover but not in general a v-cover.
items.note: Example 6.8 exhibits the failure for a rank 2 valuation ring.

items.name: Excision and formal glueing for étale cohomology
items.statement: For any torsion abelian group Λ the functor X ↦ RΓ(X_ét, Λ) is excisive on rings and satisfies formal glueing.
items.note: The concrete corollary of Theorem 1.8 that the applications in Section 6 use.

items.name: Gabber–Huber affine analogue of proper base change
items.statement: Let R be henselian along an ideal I ⊂ R and F a torsion étale sheaf on Spec(R), viewed on all Spec(R)-schemes by pullback. If R admits the structure of an algebra over a henselian local ring, then RΓ(Spec(R)_ét, F) → RΓ(Spec(R/I)_ét, F) is an equivalence.
items.note: The paper reproves this in the stated class of examples; Gabber and Huber prove it without the hypothesis that R be an algebra over a henselian local ring.

items.name: Fujiwara–Gabber base change for the complement of a henselian pair
items.statement: Let R be henselian along a finitely generated ideal I and F a torsion étale sheaf on Spec(R). Then RΓ((Spec(R) \ V(I))_ét, F) → RΓ((Spec(R̂_I) \ V(IR̂_I))_ét, F) is an equivalence.
items.locator: arXiv:1807.04725v4 (14 December 2020), Corollary 1.18(2) (= Theorem 6.11; Fujiwara, Gabber)
items.note: Reproved here from arc-descent; in the literature the noetherian case is Fujiwara's and the general case is Gabber's ([Travaux, Exp. XX, §4.4]).

items.name: Artin–Grothendieck vanishing for affinoids
items.statement: Fix a complete algebraically closed nonarchimedean field K and a classical affinoid K-algebra A of dimension d, a prime ℓ and an ℓ-power torsion étale sheaf F on Spec(A). If A is smooth or if ℓ is not the residue characteristic of K, then H^i(Spec(A)_ét, F) = 0 for i > d; in general H^i(Spec(A)_ét, F) = 0 for i > d + 1.
items.note: The final application, extending results of Hansen; the proof runs through arc-descent, a Künneth formula and analytic descent.

items.name: Every v-cover is an arc-cover
items.statement: Let f : Y → X be a v-cover of qcqs schemes. Then f is an arc-cover.
items.note: The arc-topology is finer than the v-topology; the proof produces, from a rank 1 valuation ring downstairs, a rank 1 valuation ring upstairs by localising and quotienting a lift.

items.name: Immediate specialisations in valuation rings
items.statement: For a valuation ring W and a nonunit f ∈ W, the ideal q = √(fW) is the minimal prime containing f and q_0 = ∩_n f^nW is the maximal prime contained in fW; if f is nonzero and not invertible the specialisation q_0 ⇝ q is immediate, i.e. (W/q_0)_q has rank 1 with pseudouniformizer f. Consequently every nontrivial specialisation p ⇝ p' in a valuation ring factors as p ⇝ q_0 ⇝ q ⇝ p' with the middle one immediate, so the spectra of valuation rings are not arbitrary totally ordered sets with least and greatest elements.
items.note: The mechanism that produces rank 1 valuation rings out of arbitrary ones; it is used throughout Sections 2 and 4.

items.name: Arc-covers are detected by the first factor of a composite
items.statement: For a composite Y' → Y → X of qcqs schemes, if the composite is an arc-cover then so is Y → X.
items.note: One of the sorites for arc-covers.

items.name: Criterion for a cover of a rank 1 valuation ring
items.statement: Let (V, m) be a rank 1 valuation ring and A a V-algebra with structure map f. The following are equivalent: Spec(A) → Spec(V) is a v-cover; it is an arc-cover; there are primes p_1 ⊂ p_2 of A with f^{-1}(p_1) = 0 and f^{-1}(p_2) = m, i.e. the specialisation (0) ⇝ m lifts to Spec(A).
items.note: The rank 1 case, from which the general comparison of the two topologies is deduced.

items.name: Arc-covers are detected after base change to rank ≤ 1 valuation rings
items.statement: A map f : Y → X of qcqs schemes is an arc-cover if and only if every base change of f along a map Spec(V) → X, for V a rank ≤ 1 valuation ring, is a v-cover.
items.note: Reduces arc-covers to v-covers over rank ≤ 1 bases.

items.name: The two topologies agree over a noetherian base
items.statement: Let f : Y → X be a map of qcqs schemes with X noetherian. Then f is a v-cover if and only if it is an arc-cover.
items.note: The arc-topology differs from the v-topology only in the non-noetherian world.

items.name: An excision datum gives an arc-cover
items.statement: For an excision datum f : (A, I) → (B, J), the map A → A/I × B is an arc-cover; more precisely, every map from A to a rank ≤ 1 valuation ring factors through A/I × B.
items.note: The precise reason arc-sheaves are excisive.

items.name: Excision data attached to valuation rings
items.statement: Let V be a valuation ring and p ⊂ q primes of V. Then (V_q, pV_q) → (V_p, pV_p) is an excision datum.
items.note: The universal example of an excision datum, and the square appearing in the arc-descent criterion.

items.name: Localisation and quotient form an arc-cover
items.statement: For a valuation ring V and a prime p ⊂ V, the map V → V_p × V/p is an arc-cover.
items.note: The basic arc-cover; also deducible from [Pic, Corollary 33].

items.name: Affine arc-covers and universal injectivity
items.statement: For a map f : Spec(B) → Spec(A) of affine schemes, f is an arc-cover if and only if A → B becomes universally injective after every base change along a map A → V with V a rank ≤ 1 valuation ring.
items.note: A ring-theoretic characterisation of affine arc-covers.

items.name: Submersions and universal submersions
items.statement: A map f : X → Y of qcqs schemes is submersive if it induces a quotient map of underlying topological spaces, i.e. is surjective and Y carries the quotient topology; it is universally submersive if every base change along a map of qcqs schemes is submersive.
items.note: Classical topology of schemes; the arc-topology is characterised by a refinement of it.

items.name: v-covers are universally submersive
items.statement: Every v-cover f : X → Y of qcqs schemes is universally submersive.
items.note: The topological content of v-covers.

items.name: Spectral submersions
items.statement: A map f : X → Y of qcqs schemes is spectrally submersive if it is surjective and, for every subset U ⊂ Y whose preimage f^{-1}(U) is quasi-compact open, U is open (hence quasi-compact); it is universally spectrally submersive if every base change along a map of qcqs schemes is spectrally submersive.
items.note: The topological notion that exactly matches arc-covers (Proposition 2.19); it is weaker than being a quotient map, as Remark 2.18 shows.

items.name: A constructible criterion for spectral submersions
items.statement: For a surjective map f : X → Y of qcqs schemes, condition (2) of Definition 2.14 may be relaxed to: for every constructible U ⊂ Y with f^{-1}(U) open, U is open. The proof uses that a surjective spectral map induces a quotient map for the constructible topology, so a set with constructible preimage is constructible.
items.note: The workable form of the definition, and the reason the notion is stable under the limits of Lemma 2.17.

items.name: Universal spectral submersions are local for the v-topology
items.statement: Universally spectrally submersive maps are closed under composition and base change, so the property may be checked Zariski-locally, or even v-locally, on the source and the target: given a square with X' → X and Y' → Y v-covers, f : X → Y is universally spectrally submersive if f' : X' → Y' is.
items.note: Used to reduce the characterisation of arc-covers to a local computation.

items.name: Spectral submersions are stable under cofiltered limits
items.statement: If f : X → Y is a cofiltered inverse limit of maps f_i : X_i → Y_i of qcqs schemes along affine transition maps and each f_i is a spectral submersion (resp. a universal spectral submersion), then so is f.
items.note: This is exactly what fails for ordinary submersions, as Remark 2.18 shows.

items.name: A universal spectral submersion that is not a quotient map
items.statement: There is a valuation ring V whose spectrum is the totally ordered set {0} ∪ {1/n : n ≥ 1} with 0 the generic point; with V_n = (V/p_n)_{p_{n-1}} for n > 1 and V_1 = κ(p_1), the map V → B = ∏_n V_n gives f : Spec(B) → Spec(V) which is an arc-cover and a universal spectral submersion, but not a quotient map: π_0(Spec B) = βN and f^{-1}((0)) is the preimage of βN − N, so the generic point would be closed. Writing V as a filtered colimit of finite rank valuation rings W_i, each Spec(B) → Spec(W_i) is a universal submersion while the limit is not a quotient map.
items.note: The counterexample separating submersions from spectral submersions, and an acceptance test for any formalisation.

items.name: Arc-covers are exactly the universal spectral submersions
items.statement: A map f : X → Y of qcqs schemes is universally spectrally submersive if and only if it is an arc-cover.
items.note: A purely topological characterisation of the arc-topology.

items.name: Arc-covers are stable under cofiltered limits
items.statement: The collection of arc-covers of qcqs schemes is closed under filtered inverse limits with affine transition maps.
items.note: Immediate from Proposition 2.19 and Lemma 2.17; false for v-covers.

items.name: Valuation subrings cut out by a subfield
items.statement: Let W be a valuation ring with fraction field K and K_0 ⊂ K a subfield. Then W_0 = K_0 ∩ W is a valuation ring and W_0 → W is faithfully flat; if K_0 is algebraically closed then W_0 is absolutely integrally closed.
items.note: Used to bound the cardinality of the valuation rings needed in Section 3.

items.name: Every valuation ring is a filtered colimit of finite rank ones
items.statement: Every valuation ring V is a filtered colimit of valuation subrings V_i ⊂ V such that each V_i has finite rank and each map V_i → V_j is faithfully flat; if V is absolutely integrally closed the V_i may also be taken absolutely integrally closed.
items.note: Reduces statements about arbitrary valuation rings to the finite rank case.

items.name: v-sheaves, arc-sheaves and finitary functors
items.statement: For a ring R and an ∞-category C with small limits, F : Sch_{qcqs,R}^op → C is a v-sheaf (resp. arc-sheaf) if it carries finite disjoint unions to products and, for every v-cover (resp. arc-cover) Y → X, F(X) → lim(F(Y) ⇉ F(Y ×_X Y) ⇛ …) is an equivalence. If C has filtered colimits, F is finitary if for every cofiltered tower {Y_α} of qcqs R-schemes with affine transition maps, colim_α F(Y_α) → F(lim_α Y_α) is an equivalence; a finitary functor is determined by its restriction to R-schemes of finite presentation.
items.note: The finitariness hypothesis is what allows limit arguments and Stacks 09MU relative approximation; all the paper's criteria assume it.

items.name: Universal F-descent
items.statement: A map f : Y → X in Sch_{qcqs,R} is of F-descent if F(X) → lim(F(Y) ⇉ F(Y ×_X Y) ⇛ …) is an equivalence, and of universal F-descent if every base change f' : Y' → X' along a map X' → X is of F-descent.
items.note: The relative notion in which all the detection arguments of Section 3 are phrased.

items.name: Étale and proper surjections are of universal descent for étale cohomology
items.statement: For an abelian group A and F(X) = RΓ(X_ét, A) valued in D(Z), every étale surjection is of universal F-descent (a general fact about cohomology on a site) and, for A torsion, every proper surjection is of universal F-descent by proper cohomological descent.
items.note: The classical inputs; Proposition 5.2 generalises them to v-covers.

items.name: Sorites for universal descent
items.statement: For maps f : Y → X and g : Z → Y: (1) if f has a section then f is of universal F-descent; (2) if f and g are of universal F-descent then so is f ∘ g; (3) if f ∘ g is of universal F-descent then so is f; (4) maps of universal F-descent are stable under base change.
items.note: The formal properties used constantly in Sections 3–5.

items.name: ∞-categories compactly generated by cotruncated objects
items.statement: An ∞-category C is compactly generated by cotruncated objects if it is compactly generated (presentable and generated under colimits by its compact objects) and every compact x ∈ C is n-cotruncated for some n, i.e. Hom_C(x, y) is n-truncated for all y ∈ C.
items.note: The standing hypothesis on the target category of a sheaf in this paper; it is what makes totalizations commute with filtered colimits.

items.name: Examples of compact generation by cotruncated objects
items.statement: The coconnective derived ∞-category D(Λ)^{≥0} of a ring Λ (compact objects τ^{≥0}P for P perfect), the ∞-category S_{≤n} of n-truncated spaces, and the ∞-category Cat_n of (n,1)-categories are compactly generated by cotruncated objects; the unbounded versions D(Λ), S and Cat_∞ are not.
items.note: Delimits the scope of the main theorems: they apply to coconnective coefficients and to bounded categorical targets.

items.name: Totalizations commute with filtered colimits
items.statement: Let C be compactly generated by cotruncated objects. Then totalizations in C commute with filtered colimits; consequently, for a finitary F : Sch_{qcqs,R}^op → C, the maps of universal F-descent (resp. F-descent) are closed under filtered limits with affine transition maps.
items.note: The technical heart of the finitary formalism.

items.name: v-sheaves are detected on finitely presented schemes
items.statement: Let C be compactly generated by cotruncated objects. A finitary functor F : Sch_{qcqs,R}^op → C is a v-sheaf if and only if it carries finite disjoint unions of finitely presented R-schemes to products and satisfies descent for every v-cover of finitely presented R-schemes.
items.note: With Corollary 3.9 it identifies finitary v-sheaves on qcqs schemes with v-sheaves on finitely presented schemes, which is how h-sheaves are promoted to v-sheaves in Section 5.

items.name: Finitary v-sheaves are v-sheaves on finitely presented schemes
items.statement: For C compactly generated by cotruncated objects, the ∞-category of finitary C-valued v-sheaves on Sch_{qcqs,R} is equivalent to the ∞-category of C-valued v-sheaves on finitely presented R-schemes.
items.note: The restriction/left Kan extension equivalence used for h-differentials in Section 5.3.

items.name: Sheaves on a profinite set are determined on clopens
items.statement: For X a profinite set with poset B of quasi-compact (equivalently clopen) opens, restriction identifies the ∞-category of C-valued sheaves on X with the ∞-category of functors B^op → C carrying finite disjoint unions to products.
items.note: The basic fact about profinite sets that makes ultraproducts behave like stalks.

items.name: Sheaves on the power set of a set
items.statement: For a set T with poset P(T) of all subsets, a functor f : P(T)^op → C is a sheaf if it carries finite disjoint unions to products; the basic example is f(T') = ∏_{t ∈ T'} u(t) attached to a functor u : T → C.
items.note: The combinatorial model of a sheaf on βT.

items.name: Stalks at ultrafilters
items.statement: With the clopen algebra of βT identified with P(T), sheaves on P(T) are sheaves on βT, and for a sheaf f : P(T)^op → C and an ultrafilter U on T the stalk is f_U = colim_{T' ∈ U} f(T'), the colimit over the filtered poset of members of U.
items.note: The construction that turns ultraproducts into stalks.

items.name: Equivalences of sheaves are detected on stalks
items.statement: For C compactly generated and a map η : f → g of sheaves in Fun(P(T)^op, C), η is an equivalence if and only if η_U : f_U → g_U is an equivalence for every ultrafilter U on T.
items.note: The detection principle behind Corollaries 3.18 and 3.19.

items.name: Ultraproducts of rings
items.statement: For a family {A_t}_{t ∈ T} of R-algebras and an ultrafilter U on T, the ultraproduct is ∏_U A_t = colim_{T' ∈ U} ∏_{t ∈ T'} A_t, a filtered colimit.
items.note: LD.0 plans ultraproducts and Łoś's theorem for first-order structures; the ring-theoretic ultraproduct and its geometric description are what this paper needs.

items.name: Ultraproducts via the spectrum of a product
items.statement: For commutative rings {A_t}_{t ∈ T}, Spec(∏_t A_t) carries a natural projection to βT whose fibre over a quasi-compact open corresponding to T' ⊂ T is the clopen subscheme Spec(∏_{T'} A_t); the ultraproduct ∏_U A_t is the coordinate ring of the closed pro-open subscheme π^{-1}(U). Explicitly, a prime p ⊂ ∏_t A_t maps to the ultrafilter of subsets T' whose characteristic function does not lie in p.
items.note: Identifies the ultraproduct as a localisation of a product, which is how it enters descent arguments.

items.name: Ultraproducts as stalks of a functor
items.statement: Let {A_t} be a family of R-algebras and F : Ring_R → C a functor preserving finite products and filtered colimits. Then T' ↦ F(∏_{T'} A_t) is a sheaf on P(T) whose stalk at U is F(∏_U A_t); the same holds for T' ↦ F(B ⊗_A ∏_{T'} A_t) for an A-algebra B, with stalk F(B ⊗_A ∏_U A_t).
items.note: The bridge from ultraproducts to descent statements about ∏_t A_t.

items.name: Ultraproducts detect equivalences on a product
items.statement: Let C be compactly generated and presentable and F_a, F_b : Ring_R → C commute with filtered colimits and finite products. If F_a(∏_U A_t) → F_b(∏_U A_t) is an equivalence for every ultrafilter U on T, then F_a(∏_T A_t) → F_b(∏_T A_t) is an equivalence.
items.note: The workhorse of Section 3.2.

items.name: Truncatedness passes from ultraproducts to products
items.statement: Let F : Ring_R → S commute with filtered colimits and finite products. If F(∏_U A_t) is n-truncated for every ultrafilter U on T (with n fixed), then F(∏_T A_t) is n-truncated.
items.note: Used for the truncatedness criteria of Section 4.

items.name: Detection of universal F-descent
items.statement: A family {X_i → X} of qcqs R-schemes detects universal F-descent if a map f : Y → X is of universal F-descent precisely when each base change Y ×_X X_i → X_i is.
items.note: The device that reduces descent statements to valuation rings.

items.name: Basic detection families
items.statement: A map of universal F-descent detects universal F-descent; detection is transitive along families; and if {Spec(A_i) → Spec(A)} detects universal F-descent then Spec(∏_i A_i) → Spec(A) is of universal F-descent, since it has a section after base change to each Spec(A_j).
items.note: The elementary sorites of detection, with the converse supplied by Lemma 3.25.

items.name: Detection and filtered limits
items.statement: Let C be compactly generated by cotruncated objects and F : Sch_{qcqs,R}^op → C finitary. Let X = lim_{j ∈ J} X_j be a filtered limit with affine transition maps and {Y_i} a family of qcqs X-schemes. If for each j the family {Y_i → X_j} detects universal F-descent, then so does {Y_i → X}.
items.note: Allows detection to be checked after approximating by finitely presented objects.

items.name: Ultraproducts detect universal descent
items.statement: Let C be compactly generated by cotruncated objects, F : Ring_R → C finitary and product-preserving, {A_t}_{t ∈ T} a family of R-algebras and A = ∏_t A_t. Then the maps {A → ∏_U A_t}, for U ranging over the ultrafilters on T, detect universal F-descent.
items.note: The converse to Example 3.23; it is what makes the valuation-ring detection of Proposition 3.30 possible.

items.name: Absolutely integrally closed rings
items.statement: A ring R is absolutely integrally closed if every monic polynomial in R[x] has a root in R.
items.note: PerfectoidQuotients Q3 proves that integral perfectoid rings admit absolutely integrally closed perfectoid extensions, but the general notion and its valuation-theoretic properties are not planned in the atlas.

items.name: Ultraproducts of aic valuation rings
items.statement: An ultraproduct of absolutely integrally closed valuation rings is an absolutely integrally closed valuation ring.
items.note: First-order transfer for valuation rings; together with Lemma 3.25 it produces the detecting families of valuation rings.

items.name: Every valuation ring admits a faithfully flat aic extension
items.statement: For every valuation ring V there is an absolutely integrally closed valuation ring V' and a faithfully flat (hence v-covering) map V → V'.
items.note: Reduces v-descent statements to absolutely integrally closed valuation rings.

items.name: Cardinality bound for aic valuation rings
items.statement: Let A be a commutative ring and κ = max(card(A), ℵ_0). For every absolutely integrally closed valuation ring W with a map A → W there is a factorisation A → W' → W with W' an absolutely integrally closed valuation ring of cardinality ≤ κ and W' → W faithfully flat.
items.note: Turns a proper class of valuation rings into a set, which the detection arguments need.

items.name: Detection by absolutely integrally closed valuation rings
items.statement: Let C be compactly generated by cotruncated objects and F : Sch_{qcqs,R}^op → C a finitary v-sheaf. For every R-algebra A there is a set of maps {A → V_i}_{i ∈ S} with each V_i an absolutely integrally closed valuation ring, such that the family detects universal F-descent and A → ∏_{i ∈ S} V_i is a v-cover.
items.note: The main detection theorem of Section 3.

items.name: Maps of finitary v-sheaves are detected on aic valuation rings
items.statement: Let C be compactly generated by cotruncated objects and f : F → G a map of finitary v-sheaves on Sch_{qcqs,R}. Then f is an equivalence if and only if F(Spec V) → G(Spec V) is an equivalence for every absolutely integrally closed valuation ring V that is an R-algebra.
items.note: The comparison principle used to identify arc-sheafifications in Sections 5 and 6.

items.name: Valuation rings are not enough for the arc-topology
items.statement: For every commutative ring A there is a v-cover A → B each of whose connected components is a valuation ring; by contrast, already for A = k[x, y] there is no arc-cover A → B with that property.
items.note: Marks the limit of the valuation-ring technique in the arc-topology.

items.name: The main theorem: arc-descent equals excision equals aic-v-excision
items.statement: Let C be compactly generated by cotruncated objects and F : Sch_{qcqs,R}^op → C a finitary functor satisfying v-descent. Then the following are equivalent: (1) F satisfies arc-descent; (2) F satisfies excision; (3) F satisfies aic-v-excision, i.e. for every absolutely integrally closed valuation ring V that is an R-algebra and every prime p ⊂ V, the square F(V) → F(V/p), F(V_p) → F(κ(p)) is cartesian.
items.note: The main theorem of the paper: a single Milnor square for aic valuation rings upgrades v-descent to arc-descent.

items.name: Arc-descent implies aic-v-excision
items.statement: If F satisfies arc-descent then F satisfies aic-v-excision.
items.note: The easy implication, from Corollary 2.9 and Proposition 2.8.

items.name: Primes in extensions of aic valuation rings
items.statement: Let V → W be a map of absolutely integrally closed valuation rings and p ⊂ V a prime with pW ≠ W. Then pW ⊂ W is prime with contraction p, and there is a largest prime q ⊂ W contracting to p, for which W ⊗_V V_p ≅ W_q and W ⊗_V κ(p) ≅ W_q/pW_q.
items.note: The base-change computation that makes aic-v-excision stable under extension.

items.name: aic-v-excision holds after arbitrary base change
items.statement: Let V be an absolutely integrally closed valuation ring, A a V-algebra and F : Sch_{qcqs,V}^op → C a finitary v-sheaf satisfying aic-v-excision, with C compactly generated by cotruncated objects. Then for every prime p ⊂ V the map F(A) → F(A ⊗_V V_p) ×_{F(A ⊗_V κ(p))} F(A/p) is an equivalence.
items.note: Propagates the single excision square to all A, using Lemma 4.3 and detection by valuation rings.

items.name: v-covers descend along filtered colimits of finitely presented maps
items.statement: Let {A_i → B_i} be a filtered diagram of finitely presented ring maps with A_j ⊗_{A_i} B_i ≅ B_j for every i → j. If colim A_i → colim B_i is a v-cover then A_j → B_j is a v-cover for some, hence all sufficiently large, j.
items.note: An approximation statement for v-covers.

items.name: Intervals in the spectrum of a valuation ring
items.statement: For primes p ⊂ q of a valuation ring V, the interval I = [p, q] is the set of primes between them, equal to Spec((V/p)_q), with associated valuation ring V_I = (V/p)_q; intervals are partially ordered by inclusion, [p, q] ⊂ [p', q'] iff p ⊃ p' and q ⊂ q'; I ↦ V_I is contravariant, every chain of intervals has a supremum and an infimum, and the infimum (intersection) corresponds to the filtered colimit of the V_I.
items.note: The induction device for the proof of the main theorem.

items.name: The interval induction principle
items.statement: Let V be a valuation ring and P a collection of intervals of Spec(V) such that: every interval of length ≤ 1 lies in P; P is closed under subintervals; every non-maximal prime p admits q ⊋ p with [p, q] ∈ P; every nonzero prime p admits r ⊊ p with [r, p] ∈ P; and P is closed under unions of overlapping intervals. Then P consists of all intervals of Spec(V).
items.note: A transfinite induction along the totally ordered spectrum of a valuation ring; the combinatorial core of the proof of Theorem 4.1.

items.name: aic-v-excision implies arc-descent
items.statement: Let C be compactly generated by cotruncated objects and F : Sch_{qcqs,R}^op → C a finitary v-sheaf satisfying aic-v-excision. Then F is an arc-sheaf.
items.note: The hard implication of Theorem 4.1, proved by the interval induction of Lemma 4.7.

items.name: Contractibility criterion for arc-sheaves of spaces
items.statement: Let V be an absolutely integrally closed valuation ring and F : Ring_V → S a finitary arc-sheaf such that for every interval I ⊂ Spec(V) the space F(V_I) is discrete, and is contractible when I has length ≤ 1. Then F(V) is contractible.
items.note: A space-level form of the interval induction.

items.name: Truncatedness is detected on rank ≤ 1 valuation rings
items.statement: Let F : Ring_R → S_{≤n} be a finitary arc-sheaf such that F(W) is k-truncated (−1 ≤ k ≤ n) for every absolutely integrally closed rank ≤ 1 valuation ring W that is an R-algebra. Then F(R') is k-truncated for every R-algebra R'.
items.note: Used for the categorical examples of Section 5.

items.name: Maps of arc-sheaves are detected on rank ≤ 1 aic valuation rings
items.statement: Let C be compactly generated by cotruncated objects and F_1 → F_2 a map of finitary arc-sheaves on Sch_{qcqs,R} such that F_1(W) → F_2(W) is an equivalence for every absolutely integrally closed rank ≤ 1 valuation ring W that is an R-algebra. Then F_1 → F_2 is an equivalence.
items.note: The arc-analogue of Proposition 3.32, and the practical tool for identifying arc-sheaves.

items.name: A variant with extensions
items.statement: Same hypotheses as Corollary 4.11, except that for every such W one only requires an extension W → W' of rank ≤ 1 valuation rings with F_1(W') → F_2(W') an equivalence. Then F_1 → F_2 is an equivalence.
items.note: The form used in Section 6 for rigid-analytic statements.

items.name: Milnor squares base change to Milnor squares over domains
items.statement: For a Milnor square attached to an excision datum (A, I) → (B, J) and any map A → V with V an integral domain, the base change of the square along A → V is again a Milnor square.
items.note: Elementary commutative algebra of Milnor squares; the layer that plans excision in K-theory (K.5) is where it belongs.

items.name: v-sheaves are excisive for surjective excision data
items.statement: Let C be compactly generated by cotruncated objects and F : Sch_{qcqs,R}^op → C a finitary v-sheaf. Then F carries every base change of a Milnor square with A → B surjective to a pullback square.
items.note: The case of excision that already follows from v-descent; the remaining case is what needs the arc-topology.

items.name: Finitary arc-sheaves are excisive
items.statement: Let C be compactly generated by cotruncated objects and F : Sch_{qcqs,R}^op → C a finitary arc-sheaf. Then F is excisive.
items.note: The finitary half of Theorem 1.12; Corollary 4.25 removes the finitariness hypothesis by a topos-theoretic argument.

items.name: The arc-topos on schemes of bounded size
items.statement: Fix an uncountable strong limit cardinal κ and a base ring R of cardinality < κ, and let Sch_{qcqs,R,<κ} be the category of qcqs R-schemes that are finite unions of affines with coordinate rings of cardinality < κ. The arc-topology on it has as covering families {U_i → U} those admitting a finite subfamily with the arc-lifting property against rank ≤ 1 valuation rings of size < κ; Shv_arc(Sch_{qcqs,R,<κ}) denotes the resulting topos.
items.note: The set-theoretic bookkeeping needed to sheafify; Remarks 4.17 and 4.18 show the notion of covering and the resulting theory are independent of κ in the relevant sense.

items.name: Independence of the cardinal bound
items.statement: Since κ is a strong limit cardinal, the constructions of valuation rings from schemes preserve size < κ, so the covering families of Definition 4.16 do not depend on κ; and for κ' > κ the inclusion Sch_{qcqs,R,<κ} ⊂ Sch_{qcqs,R,<κ'} induces a comparison of the associated arc-topoi.
items.note: Makes 'the' arc-topos meaningful.

items.name: The arc-topos is coherent and has enough points
items.statement: The topos Shv_arc(Sch_{qcqs,R,<κ}) is coherent; the arc-sheafification h_X^♯ of a representable is a coherent object; an object F is coherent if and only if there is a surjection h_X^♯ → F with h_X^♯ ×_F h_X^♯ quasi-compact; and the topos has enough points.
items.note: Puts Deligne-style coherence arguments at the disposal of the arc-topology.

items.name: The arc-topology is not subcanonical
items.statement: The arc-topology is not subcanonical, so sheafification is necessary in the statements of Lemma 4.19(2) and (3).
items.note: A caution that distinguishes the arc-topology from the fpqc and v-topologies in this respect.

items.name: Surjectivity and isomorphy criteria for coherent arc-sheaves
items.statement: Let F → G be a map of arc-sheaves of sets on Sch_{qcqs,R,<κ}. (1) If G is coherent and F quasi-compact, then F → G is surjective if and only if it has the arc-lifting property against rank ≤ 1 valuation rings of size < κ. (2) If F and G are coherent, then F ≅ G if and only if F(V) ≅ G(V) for a cofinal collection of such valuation rings.
items.note: The set-level detection principle for the arc-topos.

items.name: Detecting surjections and isomorphisms after sheafification
items.statement: Let F_0 → G_0 be a map of presheaves of sets on Sch_{qcqs,R,<κ} whose arc-sheafifications are coherent. If for every rank ≤ 1 valuation ring V of size < κ there is an extension V → W of rank ≤ 1 valuation rings of size < κ with F_0(W) → G_0(W) surjective (resp. bijective), then F_0^♯ → G_0^♯ is surjective (resp. bijective).
items.note: The tool used to identify the pushout squares of Proposition 4.24 and Theorem 6.6.

items.name: Coherence of a pushout
items.statement: In Shv_arc(Sch_{qcqs,R,<κ}), if A → B is injective and A, B, C are coherent, then the pushout D of C ← A → B is coherent.
items.note: A coherence criterion needed to apply Lemma 4.21 to excision squares.

items.name: Excision squares become pushouts of arc-sheaves
items.statement: For an excision datum (A, I) → (B, J) with A, B of size < κ, the arc-sheafification of the square Spec(B/J) → Spec(B), Spec(A/I) → Spec(A) is a pushout square both in the topos of arc-sheaves of sets and in the ∞-topos of arc-sheaves of spaces.
items.note: The topos-theoretic form of excision; it removes the finitariness hypothesis.

items.name: Every arc-sheaf is excisive
items.statement: Let F be a sheaf on Sch_{qcqs,R,<κ} valued in an ∞-category C with all small limits. Then F carries excision squares to pullback squares, i.e. satisfies excision.
items.note: Theorem 1.12 in full generality, without finitariness.

items.name: Descent is detected on strict henselizations
items.statement: Let F : Sch_{qcqs,R}^op → D(Λ)^{≥0} be finitary and satisfy étale descent. If f : Y → X is such that the base changes of f to the strict henselizations of X are of F-descent, then f is of F-descent.
items.note: The standard reduction to strictly henselian local rings, in the ∞-categorical setting.

items.name: v-descent for étale cohomology
items.statement: Let G be a torsion sheaf on Spec(R)_ét and F the functor (f : X → Spec(R)) ↦ RΓ(X_ét, f^*G) valued in D(Λ)^{≥0}. Then F satisfies v-descent.
items.note: The v-sheaf property of étale cohomology, the input to which the arc-criterion is applied.

items.name: aic valuation rings are strictly henselian
items.statement: An absolutely integrally closed valuation ring is strictly henselian.
items.note: Why the excision square of Theorem 4.1 can be computed in étale cohomology.

items.name: arc-descent for étale cohomology
items.statement: Let G be a torsion sheaf on Spec(R)_ét and F(f : X → Spec(R)) = RΓ(X_ét, f^*G) valued in D(Λ)^{≥0}. Then F satisfies arc-descent; in particular it satisfies excision.
items.note: The main example; with Theorem 4.1 its proof is the computation of étale cohomology of an aic valuation ring and its quotients.

items.name: Excision for étale cohomology from rigidity
items.statement: For an excision datum (A, I) → (B, J), the square of RΓ(−, Λ) is cartesian: excision data are preserved by flat base change in A, so one may localise and assume A strictly henselian local, and then rigidity for henselian pairs identifies the relevant cohomologies.
items.note: A direct proof of excision for étale cohomology, independent of the general machine.

items.name: Rydh's theorem: étale objects are arc-sheaves
items.statement: The following are finitary arc-sheaves: X ↦ the category of étale qcqs X-schemes separated over X; X ↦ the category of finite étale X-schemes; X ↦ the category of constructible étale sheaves of sets on X, equivalently of étale qcqs algebraic spaces over X.
items.note: The categorical (1-truncated) examples; their proof uses the truncatedness criterion of Lemma 4.10.

items.name: Separated étale schemes over an aic valuation ring
items.statement: Let V be an absolutely integrally closed valuation ring and f : X → Spec(V) a quasi-compact separated étale morphism. Then X is a disjoint union of V-schemes of the form Spec(V[1/t]), t ∈ V; equivalently, separated étale V-schemes are the disjoint unions of quasi-compact opens of Spec(V).
items.note: The computation that makes Rydh's theorem accessible to the arc-criterion.

items.name: Constructible complexes and their amplitude filtration
items.statement: For a qcqs scheme X and a coefficient ring Λ, D^b_cons(X_ét, Λ) is the full subcategory of the derived ∞-category of étale sheaves of Λ-modules spanned by bounded objects with constructible cohomology, and D^b_cons(X_ét, Λ)^{[-n,n]} the objects of amplitude in [−n, n]; for n = 0 this is the abelian category of constructible sheaves.
items.note: The target of the second descent theorem; Remark 5.9 discusses the comparison with the standard definition when Λ has a nontrivial Jacobson radical.

items.name: Constructible complexes form a finitary functor
items.statement: The functor X ↦ D^b_cons(X_ét, Λ) is finitary, and so is X ↦ D^b_cons(X_ét, Λ)^{[-n,n]} for each n.
items.note: Limit-compatibility of constructible complexes, needed to apply the criterion.

items.name: Constructible complexes form a hypercomplete v-sheaf
items.statement: The functor X ↦ D^b_cons(X, Λ) on Sch_qcqs is a hypercomplete v-sheaf, and so is X ↦ D^b_cons(X, Λ)^{[-n,n]} for each n.
items.note: The v-descent half of Theorem 5.13.

items.name: Constructible complexes on the spectrum of a finite-rank aic valuation ring
items.statement: Let V be an absolutely integrally closed valuation ring of finite rank m, so that X = Spec(V) is the poset 0 → 1 → … → m under specialisation. Then D^b_cons(X_ét, Λ) is the ∞-category of functors (0 → 1 → … → m)^op → D^b_fg(Λ), and similarly with amplitude restrictions.
items.note: The explicit computation from which the excision square is read off.

items.name: arc-descent for constructible complexes
items.statement: The functor X ↦ D^b_cons(X_ét, Λ) is a hypercomplete arc-sheaf, and so is X ↦ D^b_cons(X_ét, Λ)^{[-n,n]} for each n.
items.note: The sheaf-level strengthening of Theorem 5.4, and the second half of Theorem 1.8.

items.name: h-differentials as a functor on qcqs schemes
items.statement: For k of characteristic zero, the Huber–Jörder h-differentials RΓ_h(X, Ω^i_h) ∈ D(k) of a finite type k-scheme define an h-sheaf which for smooth X agrees with RΓ_Zar(X, Ω^i); F_i : Sch_{qcqs,k}^op → D(k) is its left Kan extension, so F_i(X) = colim_j RΓ_h(X_j, Ω^i_h) for X = lim_j X_j a filtered limit of finite type k-schemes with affine transition maps.
items.note: The third example of an arc-sheaf, suggested by Ayoub.

items.name: h-differentials satisfy arc-descent
items.statement: The functor F_i : Sch_{qcqs,k}^op → D(k) of h-differential i-forms is an arc-sheaf.
items.note: Its proof uses that valuation k-algebras in characteristic zero are ind-smooth (local uniformization; in the aic case, alterations), so F_i(Spec R) = Ω^i_{R/k}, and that p = p² in an aic valuation ring gives the required pullback square of differentials.

items.name: The de Rham-type functor is an arc-sheaf
items.statement: The construction X ↦ F(X) assembled from the h-differentials defines an arc-sheaf.
items.note: The packaged form of Theorem 5.14.

items.name: arc-hyperdescent for perfect complexes on perfect schemes
items.statement: Fix a prime p and let F carry a qcqs F_p-scheme X to the ∞-category Perf(X_perf) of perfect complexes on the perfection of X. Then F is a hypercomplete arc-sheaf.
items.note: Extends v-hyperdescent for perfect complexes on perfect schemes to the arc-topology.

items.name: Universally effective epimorphisms of perfect schemes
items.statement: Fix a prime p and a qcqs algebraic space Y over F_p. The functor sending a qcqs F_p-scheme X to the set of maps X_perf → Y is an arc-sheaf of sets; moreover a map of qcqs perfect F_p-schemes Y → X is an arc-cover if and only if it is a universally effective epimorphism.
items.note: Identifies the arc-topology with the canonical topology on perfect schemes; Remark 5.18 notes that the canonical topology there is not quasi-compact.

items.name: The canonical topology on perfect schemes is not quasi-compact
items.statement: A covering family for the canonical topology on qcqs perfect F_p-schemes need not admit a finite refinement; Spec(Z) is not quasi-compact for the canonical topology ([stacks-project, Tag 0EUE]).
items.note: The precise sense in which Theorem 5.17 is sharp.

items.name: Formal glueing for nonconnective K-theory
items.statement: Nonconnective K-theory satisfies formal glueing: for a ring A and t ∈ A the square K(A) → K(Â_t), K(A[1/t]) → K(Â_t[1/t]) is homotopy cartesian, because the fibres of the horizontal maps are the K-theories of perfect t-power torsion modules over A and over Â_t ([TT, Theorem 5.1]), and those categories are equivalent; more generally the statement can be formulated for finitely generated ideals.
items.note: The motivating classical example of a formal glueing square, and an instance of what K.6's localisation sequences give; the paper's theorem recovers it for every arc-sheaf.

items.name: Completion of a rank 1 valuation ring
items.statement: Let V be a rank 1 valuation ring with pseudouniformizer t. Then the t-adic completion V̂_t is a rank 1 valuation ring and V → V̂_t is faithfully flat.
items.note: The valuation-theoretic input to Proposition 6.3.

items.name: Completion plus complement is an arc-cover
items.statement: For a ring R and a finitely generated ideal I ⊂ R, the map Spec(R̂_I) ⊔ (Spec(R) \ V(I)) → Spec(R) is an arc-cover.
items.note: The precise reason arc-sheaves satisfy formal glueing; the same map is not a v-cover (Example 6.8).

items.name: Formal glueing squares for finitary arc-sheaves
items.statement: Let C be compactly generated by cotruncated objects and F : Sch_{qcqs,R}^op → C a finitary arc-sheaf. Then for every formal glueing datum (A → B, I) of R-algebras the square F(Spec A) → F(Spec B), F(Spec A \ V(I)) → F(Spec B \ V(IB)) is cartesian.
items.note: The finitary form of Theorem 1.15; Example 6.5 specialises it to étale cohomology with I principal.

items.name: Formal glueing squares become pushouts of arc-sheaves
items.statement: For a formal glueing datum (A → B, I) with A, B of size < κ, the arc-sheafification of the square Spec(B) \ V(IB) → Spec(B), Spec(A) \ V(I) → Spec(A) is a pushout square both in the topos of arc-sheaves of sets and in the ∞-topos of arc-sheaves of spaces; consequently every arc-sheaf valued in an ∞-category with all small limits satisfies formal glueing.
items.note: Theorem 1.15 without the finitariness hypothesis.

items.name: Formal glueing fails for the v-topology
items.statement: Let V be a rank 2 valuation ring with height 1 prime p, f ∈ V − p a nonunit and I = (f). For the formal glueing datum (V → V̂_I, I) the map (Spec(V) \ V(I)) ⊔ Spec(V̂_I) → Spec(V) is not a v-cover: any valuation extension V → W would have to factor through V̂_I, which is impossible since p lies in the kernel of V → V̂_I while V → W is injective. Arc-locally there is no problem: V → V̂/p × V_p is an arc-cover factoring through it.
items.note: The counterexample promised in Remark 1.16.

items.name: Rigid functors
items.statement: A functor F on R-algebras is rigid if F(A) ≅ F(A/J) for every henselian pair (A, J) with A an R-algebra.
items.note: Rigidity plus arc-descent is what yields the Fujiwara–Gabber theorem.

items.name: Rigid arc-sheaves see only the completion
items.statement: Let R be henselian along a finitely generated ideal I and F : Sch_{qcqs,R}^op → D(Λ)^{≥0} a finitary arc-sheaf which is rigid on R-algebras. Then F(Spec(R) \ V(I)) → F(Spec(R̂_I) \ V(IR̂_I)) is an equivalence.
items.note: The abstract form of Fujiwara–Gabber.

items.name: The Fujiwara–Gabber theorem
items.statement: Let (R, I) be a henselian pair with I finitely generated and f : R → R̂_I the I-adic completion. For every torsion étale sheaf G on Spec(R) \ V(I) the map RΓ(Spec(R) \ V(I), G) → RΓ(Spec(R̂_I) \ V(IR̂_I), f^*G) is an equivalence.
items.note: Proved here from arc-descent and rigidity of étale cohomology; Fujiwara proves the noetherian case, Gabber the general one ([Travaux, Exp. XX, §4.4]).

items.name: Scope of the criterion
items.statement: The proof of Corollary 6.10 uses that equivalences in D(Λ) can be checked after pullback, so the analogous argument does not automatically apply to set-valued or category-valued functors.
items.note: A caution about extending the Fujiwara–Gabber argument to the categorical examples of Section 5.

items.name: The arc_t-topology
items.statement: A map of Z[t]-algebras R → S is an arc_t-cover if for every rank 1 valuation ring V over Z[t] in which t is a pseudouniformizer and every map R → V there is an extension V → W of rank ≤ 1 valuation rings such that R → V → W extends over S.
items.note: The variant adapted to rigid geometry; by Example 6.15 it corresponds, for Tate Huber pairs, to surjectivity of the map of adic spectra on rank 1 points, and is finer than Scholze's v-topology on affinoid rigid spaces.

items.name: arc_t-covers and adic spectra
items.statement: For a map f : (A, A^+) → (B, B^+) of Tate (Z((t)), Z[[t]])-algebras, A^+ → B^+ is an arc_t-cover if and only if Spa(f) : Spa(B, B^+) → Spa(A, A^+) is surjective on rank 1 points, equivalently the associated map of Berkovich spaces is surjective; consequently the arc_t-topology on affinoid rigid spaces is finer than the v-topology of [ScholzeDiamonds, Definition 8.1].
items.note: The dictionary between the paper's topology and the v-topology of adic spaces; it is the only point where the two frameworks are compared.

items.name: Étale cohomology of the rigid generic fibre
items.statement: For a torsion abelian group Λ, let F send a Z[t]-algebra R to RΓ(Spec(R̂_t[1/t])_ét, Λ) valued in D(Z)^{≥0}; by the Fujiwara–Gabber theorem the t-adic completion may be replaced by the t-henselization, so F commutes with filtered colimits.
items.note: The functor whose arc_t-descent gives the GAGA and Künneth statements.

items.name: arc_t-descent for the étale cohomology of affinoids
items.statement: Let A be a ring with a distinguished element t and G a torsion sheaf on Spec(A)_ét. The functor F(R) = RΓ(Spec(R̂_t[1/t]), G) on A-algebras is a finitary arc_t-sheaf.
items.note: Descent for the étale cohomology of rigid generic fibres.

items.name: GAGA for rigid étale cohomology in the proper case
items.statement: Let A be a ring with t ∈ A such that (A, (t)) is a henselian pair, and assume A noetherian or Â_t[1/t] a strongly noetherian Tate ring. For a proper A[1/t]-scheme X with associated adic space X^ad over Spa(A[1/t], A) and a torsion étale sheaf F on X with pullback F^ad, the natural map gives RΓ(X, F) ≅ RΓ(X^ad, F^ad).
items.note: The comparison of algebraic and analytic étale cohomology in the proper case, deduced from arc_t-descent.

items.name: arc_t-equivalences
items.statement: A map of A-algebras R → R' is an arc_t-equivalence if Hom_A(R, V) ≅ Hom_A(R', V) for every t-adically complete absolutely integrally closed rank ≤ 1 valuation ring V in which t is a pseudouniformizer.
items.note: The equivalence relation under which rigid étale cohomology is invariant.

items.name: Examples of arc_t-equivalences
items.statement: For an A-algebra R the following are arc_t-equivalences: R → R/(t^∞-torsion); R → R̂_t; R → R^+ the integral closure of R in R[1/t]; and, when t is a nonzerodivisor, R → R^tic where R^tic = {x ∈ R[1/t] : t^c x^N ⊂ R for some c ≥ 0} is the total integral closure, which contains the integral closure and equals it when R is noetherian.
items.note: The list of operations invisible to rigid étale cohomology.

items.name: Invariance of rigid étale cohomology under arc_t-equivalences
items.statement: Fix (A, t ∈ A) and a torsion sheaf F on Spec(A)_ét. For an arc_t-equivalence R → R' of A-algebras, RΓ(Spec(R̂_t[1/t]), F) ≅ RΓ(Spec(R̂'_t[1/t]), F).
items.note: The invariance statement used in Section 7.

items.name: Künneth formula for rigid generic fibres
items.statement: Let V be an absolutely integrally closed rank 1 valuation ring with pseudouniformizer π and ℓ a prime invertible in the residue field of V. Then F̃(R) = RΓ(Spec(R̂_π[1/π]), F_ℓ) is a symmetric monoidal functor on V-algebras: for V-algebras R, R' the natural map F̃(R) ⊗_{F_ℓ} F̃(R') → F̃(R ⊗_V R') is an equivalence.
items.note: The Künneth formula that drives the induction in Section 7; Remark 6.23 shows the hypothesis on ℓ is necessary.

items.name: v-sheaves are invariant under universal homeomorphisms
items.statement: Let Y → X be a universal homeomorphism of qcqs R-schemes. Then F(X) → F(Y) is an equivalence for every v-sheaf F valued in an ∞-category with all small limits.
items.note: The topological invariance used in the variant of excision below.

items.name: A variant of excision through the total integral closure
items.statement: Let A → B be a map of rings and t ∈ A a nonzerodivisor on A and on B with A^tic ≅ B^tic. Then for every arc-sheaf F on Ring_A valued in an ∞-category with all small limits, the square F(A) → F(A/tA), F(B) → F(B/tB) is cartesian.
items.note: An excision statement in which the two ideals are not isomorphic but the total integral closures agree.

items.name: Artin–Grothendieck vanishing in rigid geometry
items.statement: Let K be a complete algebraically closed nonarchimedean field, A a topologically finite type K-algebra of dimension d and F a torsion abelian sheaf on Spec(A)_ét. Then H^i(Spec(A), F) = 0 for i > d + 1; and if F is ℓ-power torsion with ℓ prime to the residue characteristic of K, then H^i(Spec(A), F) = 0 for i > d.
items.note: The main application, extending results of Hansen; Remark 7.4 conjectures that part (2) holds for arbitrary torsion sheaves, which amounts to the vanishing of H^{d+1} with p-power torsion coefficients.

items.name: Künneth formula for affinoid algebras
items.statement: For topologically finite type K-algebras A and B the natural map RΓ(Spec(A), F_ℓ) ⊗_{F_ℓ} RΓ(Spec(B), F_ℓ) → RΓ(Spec(A ⊗̂_K B), F_ℓ) is an equivalence in D(F_ℓ).
items.note: The affinoid form of Proposition 6.22, with ℓ prime to the residue characteristic.

items.name: Descent in the analytic topology
items.statement: Let A be a topologically finite type K-algebra and f, g ∈ A generating the unit ideal. Then for every torsion abelian sheaf F on Spec(A) the square formed by RΓ(Spec(A), F), RΓ(Spec(A⟨f/g⟩), F), RΓ(Spec(A⟨g/f⟩), F) and RΓ(Spec(A⟨f/g, g/f⟩), F) is cartesian.
items.note: Mayer–Vietoris for rational covers of affinoids, deduced from arc_t-descent; it is how the vanishing statement is localised.

items.name: Cohomology of the closed fibre as a colimit
items.statement: Let R be a topologically finite type K-algebra and f ∈ R, giving the inductive system {R⟨f/π^r⟩}. For every torsion sheaf F on Spec(R)_ét one has colim_r RΓ(Spec(R⟨f/π^r⟩), F) ≅ RΓ(Spec(R/f), F).
items.note: The limit computation that lets the induction on dimension descend to the zero locus of f.

items.name: Artin–Grothendieck vanishing for finite étale covers of rational subdomains
items.statement: Let f_1, …, f_m, g ∈ T_n generate the unit ideal and let A be finite étale over T_n⟨(f_1, …, f_m)/g⟩. Then for every torsion abelian group Λ one has RΓ(Spec(A), Λ) ∈ D(Z)^{≤n}.
items.note: The special case of the vanishing theorem proved first; the general case follows by Noether-normalisation-style arguments and the descent statements above.

items.name: Vanishing for constant coefficients
items.statement: Let R be a topologically finite type K-algebra of dimension d. Then RΓ(Spec(R), Λ) ∈ D(Z)^{≤d+1} for every torsion abelian group Λ, and RΓ(Spec(R), Λ) ∈ D(Z)^{≤d} for every ℓ-power torsion Λ with ℓ prime to the residue characteristic.
items.note: The constant-coefficient case of Theorem 7.3, from which the general case follows.

routes.title: The arc-topology and descent for étale cohomology
routes.brief: Plan the arc-topology of Bhatt and Mathew and the descent theorems it yields for étale cohomology of schemes. The final theorems are: (1) the criterion (their Theorem 4.1): for an ∞-category C compactly generated by cotruncated objects and a finitary functor F : Sch_qcqs^op → C satisfying v-descent, F satisfies arc-descent if and only if F is excisive, if and only if F satisfies aic-v-excision, i.e. for every absolutely integrally closed valuation ring V and every prime p ⊂ V the square F(V) → F(V/p), F(V_p) → F(κ(p)) is cartesian; (2) arc-descent for étale cohomology (their Theorems 5.4 and 5.13): for a torsion coefficient sheaf, X ↦ RΓ(X_ét, F) is an arc-sheaf, and for a finite ring Λ the functor X ↦ D^b_cons(X_ét, Λ) is a hypercomplete arc-sheaf; (3) the consequences (their Theorems 1.12 and 1.15, Corollaries 4.25 and 6.7): every arc-sheaf valued in an ∞-category with small limits satisfies excision for Milnor squares and formal glueing; (4) the classical applications reproved from them: the Gabber–Huber affine analogue of proper base change in the stated class of examples, the Fujiwara–Gabber theorem on the étale cohomology of the complement of a henselian pair (their Theorem 6.11), GAGA for the étale cohomology of proper rigid spaces (their Corollary 6.18), and Artin–Grothendieck vanishing for affinoids over a complete algebraically closed nonarchimedean field (their Theorem 7.3): H^i(Spec(A)_ét, F) = 0 for i > d + 1 for every torsion sheaf, and for i > d when F is ℓ-power torsion with ℓ prime to the residue characteristic. The roadmap must cover: the v-topology and the arc-topology on qcqs schemes with their comparison (a v-cover is an arc-cover; they agree over a noetherian base) and the characterisation of arc-covers as universal spectral submersions; the valuation-theoretic toolkit — rank ≤ 1 and absolutely integrally closed valuation rings, faithfully flat aic extensions, cardinality bounds, filtered colimit presentations by finite-rank subrings, and the structure of specialisations; the ∞-categorical descent formalism — finitary functors, universal F-descent and its sorites, targets compactly generated by cotruncated objects, and detection of descent by ultraproducts and by aic valuation rings; the interval induction and the proof of the criterion; the arc-topos on schemes of bounded size, its coherence, and the pushout descriptions of excision and formal glueing squares that remove the finitariness hypothesis; the examples — étale cohomology and constructible complexes, Rydh's étale objects, Huber–Jörder h-differentials in characteristic zero, and perfect complexes on perfect F_p-schemes with the identification of arc-covers as universally effective epimorphisms; and the arc_t-variant for rigid geometry with its invariance and Künneth statements, leading to the vanishing theorem of Section 7. Import, and do not re-plan: schemes, morphisms and limits of schemes from Scheme and stack foundations (SchemeAndStackFoundations), stage SF.0; fpqc/fppf descent and algebraic spaces from SF.1; the Zariski, étale, fppf and pro-étale sites of schemes, sheaf cohomology and proper and smooth base change from SF.2; constructible coefficient categories from Étale duality and perverse sheaves (EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves), stage EDC.0, and affine Artin vanishing as EDC.4 imports it; unbounded cohomological descent, Postnikov completion and hypercompleteness from Enhanced derived sheaves (EnhancedDerivedSheaves), stage E2; spectral spaces, the constructible topology and profinite techniques from Diamonds and v-stacks (DiamondsAndVStacks), stage D0; ultraproducts and Łoś's theorem from Logic and definability in number theory (LogicAndDefinabilityInNumberTheory), stage LD.0; Milnor squares, relative K-theory and excision from General algebraic K-theory (GeneralAlgebraicKTheory), stages K.5 and K.6; Tate algebras, Huber rings and topologically finite type algebras from the Tau Ceti roadmap Adic spaces, Layers 0 and 1, and adic spectra and their étale sites from Adic étale geometry (AdicEtaleGeometry), stages A0 and A1; and perfections of schemes in characteristic p from Geometric Satake and fusion (GeometricSatakeAndFusion), stage GS0:Witt-geometry. Record explicitly that the v-topology here is the one on qcqs schemes and is not the v-topology on perfectoid spaces and diamonds of DiamondsAndVStacks D2: the two have different covering conditions, and Example 6.15 of the paper is the only comparison between them.
routes.reason: Nothing in the atlas goes in this direction. The v-topology that the atlas plans (DiamondsAndVStacks D2) is Scholze's v-topology on perfectoid spaces and diamonds, a different site with a different covering condition; SchemeAndStackFoundations owns the Zariski, étale, fppf and pro-étale sites of schemes and fpqc descent, and stops there; no layer defines the h-topology, the v-topology on schemes or the arc-topology, and none plans excision, formal glueing, the Gabber–Huber and Fujiwara–Gabber theorems or Artin–Grothendieck vanishing in rigid geometry. This is a body of work with its own theorems and its own applications rather than new layers in the direction of an existing roadmap, so it is a new roadmap that imports the classical sites and descent from SchemeAndStackFoundations rather than a Part II of it.

D0 extends the spectral-space API with constructible and pro-constructible subsets, spectral maps, limits and quotient criteria, and supplies profinite decompositions and the Stone–Čech argument. The paper's submersions, spectral submersions and their stability under cofiltered limits — including the counterexample of Remark 2.18, which is exactly the 'quotients of spectral spaces' trap D0 warns about — and its description of sheaves on a profinite set and of stalks at ultrafilters are general facts of that kind, not facts about the arc-topology. The paper is a good source for them and the new roadmap should import them.

LD.0 constructs ultraproducts and proves Łoś's transfer theorem. Section 3.2 of the paper is ultraproducts of rings: their definition as a filtered colimit, their geometric description as the localisation of a product along a point of βT, the fact that an ultraproduct of absolutely integrally closed valuation rings is one again (a transfer statement), and the detection of equivalences and of truncatedness on ultraproducts. These belong in LD.0's direction, and the paper is a source for the ring-theoretic half of that layer.

K.5 plans relative K-theory of a pair (A, I) and excision under the hypotheses of an adopted theorem, and K.6 plans nonconnective K-theory with its localisation sequences. Excision data and Milnor squares are the notions those layers are about, and the formal glueing square for nonconnective K-theory of Example 6.1 is exactly the localisation-sequence statement K.6 owns. The arc-topology roadmap imports the definition and proves that every arc-sheaf satisfies excision; the K-theory layers keep ownership of the squares themselves and of the fact that K-theory does not satisfy unrestricted excision.

sourceIssues.reason: Theorem 7.3 as printed has two parts: (1) H^i = 0 for i > d + 1 for every torsion sheaf, and (2) H^i = 0 for i > d when F is ℓ-power torsion with ℓ prime to the residue characteristic. Neither mentions smoothness of A, and Remark 7.4 opens 'We would expect that part (2) of Theorem 7.3 holds for arbitrary torsion sheaves', listing the smooth constant-coefficient case as one of two special cases that are 'within reach'. No proof of the smooth case for non-constant ℓ-power torsion sheaves appears in Section 7, and the reduction of Theorem 7.3 to constant coefficients runs through Proposition 7.9 for the two cases actually stated there, not for the smooth case.
